title: Business profits
summary: Article 7 lets the source State tax business profits only through a PE, and then only the profits attributable to it. Since 2010 the Article and its Commentary follow the 'authorised OECD approach', which treats the PE as if it were a separate and independent enterprise. The Commentary also keeps a revised commentary on the earlier wording, reproduced as an Annex, for treaties that use that wording.
readingNote: Check the wording of the Saudi treaty before relying on this tab. Most Saudi treaties use the pre-2010 OECD wording, with a deductions paragraph covering 'executive and general administrative expenses', or the UN wording, which can include a limited force-of-attraction rule. For those treaties the Annex commentary at the end of this tab is the relevant OECD guidance. The main Commentary applies to treaties that copy the 2010 text, which includes a corresponding-adjustment rule in paragraph 3.

entries.t: Article 7 allocates taxing rights over business profits that no other Article covers. A State taxes another State's enterprise only through a PE there, and then only on profits attributable to it. Article 5 decides whether a PE exists but does not itself allocate taxing rights.

Attributing profits to PEs has a long history, but practice and interpretation varied widely, which caused double taxation and non-taxation. The OECD therefore developed a common approach to give taxpayers more certainty.
The 2008 report worked out the best approach without being limited by the original intent or historical practice of Article 7.

The report's full conclusions were put into a new Article 7 for new and amended treaties. A revised Commentary on the previous wording was also prepared, using the parts of the report that do not conflict with the earlier Commentary, to give certainty for existing treaties (see the Annex).

The new Article was adopted in 2010, together with a revised report (Attribution of Profits to Permanent Establishments). The Article must be read in light of that report, which covers PEs in general (Part I), banks (Part II), global trading (Part III) and insurance (Part IV).

sections.heading: Paragraph 1: the PE threshold and no general force of attraction

entries.t: Two principles. First, there is no source tax on business profits without a PE, a long-standing rule of treaty practice. Second, only profits attributable to the PE can be taxed there.

A general 'force of attraction', taxing all income from the source State once a PE exists, is now rejected in treaty practice. Some treaties keep a limited anti-avoidance version covering similar activities. Otherwise each source of profit is tested separately against the PE rule, which suits how modern businesses are organised and is simpler to administer.
Paragraph 2 defines the profits 'attributable' to the PE.
Paragraph 1 limits the source State's taxation of the other State's enterprises. It does not stop a State taxing its own residents under controlled foreign company rules (see Article 1(3)).

sections.heading: Paragraph 2: the separate and independent enterprise approach

entries.t: Profits attributable to a PE are those it would earn as a separate and independent enterprise doing the same activities in the same conditions, taking into account its functions, assets and risks. The rule does not share out the whole enterprise's profit, so a PE can show a profit even if the enterprise as a whole makes a loss, and the reverse.
Both States are bound by paragraph 2. The residence State has a direct interest in the PE State applying it correctly, because it must give relief under Article 23.

The authorised approach has two steps. First, a functional and factual analysis identifies what the PE does, which people functions, assets, risks and capital it has, and which dealings with other parts of the enterprise should be recognised. Second, transactions with associated enterprises are priced under the Transfer Pricing Guidelines, which also apply by analogy to internal dealings. The report gives sector-specific guidance for financial businesses.

Internal 'dealings' between the PE and the rest of the enterprise are recognised as if at arm's length. Because they have no legal effect, they need more scrutiny, but documentation should be no more burdensome than for associated-enterprise transactions.
Paragraph 2 applies in both States: the source State uses it to tax the PE, and the residence State uses it for relief under Articles 23 A or 23 B.

The separate-enterprise fiction only measures the PE's profit. It does not create taxable income under other Articles. A notional rent does not create Article 6 income, and a notional interest charge is not an interest payment for Article 11, so internal charges do not attract withholding under those Articles.

Some States want the fiction to apply to other Articles so that PEs are treated like subsidiaries, for example to tax internal interest. Others want to deny recognition of dealings. Either approach requires express bilateral wording.

Once the attributable profit is found, each State computes tax under its own law (depreciation, timing, deductibility), provided the result is consistent with paragraph 2. Such differences are normal and are not double taxation in themselves.
The PE State must also respect Article 24(3): expenses must be deductible on the same terms as for a domestic enterprise, however they are taken into account under Article 7.

Construction PEs often exist only after twelve months, which can cause disputes over how much profit relates to the site. Goods supplied, or services performed elsewhere, by other parts of the enterprise do not produce profits of the site PE.

The former deductions paragraph is no longer needed. Executive and general administrative expenses are now dealt with by recognising and pricing, at arm's length, the dealings through which other parts of the enterprise serve the PE.
The former paragraphs allowing apportionment of total profits and requiring the same method year by year were deleted because they do not fit the arm's length approach.

The rule that 'mere purchase' attracts no profit was also deleted. Purchasing for the enterprise is now handled by Article 5(4)(d), and where a PE exists anyway, its purchasing function is rewarded at arm's length.

sections.heading: Paragraph 3: corresponding adjustments between the two States

entries.t: Articles 7 and 23 together should prevent double taxation, but only if both States read paragraph 2 the same way. Detailed guidance and consistent taxpayer reporting usually achieve this.

Example: goods transferred from a home-country plant to a foreign PE, where both States accept the taxpayer's arm's length pricing of the dealing. Problems arise where paragraph 2 allows different acceptable methods, for example for attributing 'free' capital.
Paragraph 3 is rarely needed. It does not limit the usual remedies when a State breaches Articles 7 or 23. Where the taxpayer did not follow paragraph 2, either State may adjust.

Paragraph 3 requires the other State to make a corresponding adjustment if it agrees the first State's adjustment conforms with paragraph 2. A worked example shows both outcomes, and the rule covers cases where the two States read paragraph 2 differently.
Like Article 9(2), the obligation is reciprocal: it applies whichever State made the first adjustment.

The adjustment is not automatic. It is owed only if the other State agrees the first adjustment is justified, and only for the amount it considers correct. Where a mutual agreement fixes the amount, the first State also aligns its own adjustment so that the PE's profit is the same in both States.
Taxpayer-initiated amendments to returns that attribute profits differently can also be considered under the paragraph, subject to conditions.

The method of adjustment is not specified: an exemption State adjusts exempt profit, a credit State adjusts credit. Secondary adjustments do not arise, since no actual payment between parts of the same enterprise is involved.
Time limits for adjustments are left to domestic law or bilateral agreement. Some adjustments only change tax later, for example where losses are involved.
Disputes about the amount or character of the adjustment go to the mutual agreement procedure under Article 25.

Paragraph 3 removes only the double taxation caused by the adjustment. It applies only where the same profits are attributed to different parts of the enterprise in line with the Article, and it does not change Article 23 calculations except to give relief that would otherwise be unavailable.
Alternative wording lets States require that every corresponding adjustment be agreed through the mutual agreement procedure, with arbitration as a backstop where included.

'Profits' has a broad meaning covering all income from carrying on a business. Where a business's profits include dividends, interest or royalties, the question arises which Article applies, though it often makes no practical difference.

The specific Articles take priority over Article 7. Article 7 covers business profits outside those categories, plus items sent back to it by the PE exceptions in Articles 10(4), 11(4), 12(3) and 21(2). States remain free to classify the income as they wish for domestic purposes.
States may agree bilateral definitions, for example to separate profits from dividends.
Income from issuing or trading emissions permits and credits generally falls under Articles 7 and 13, and in some cases Articles 6, 8 or 21 (see the OECD report on emissions permits).
Two categories now fall under Article 7: equipment rentals, removed from the royalty definition, and independent personal services, which became business profits when Article 14 was removed in 2000.

sections.heading: Annex: Commentary on the previous (pre-2010) wording
sections.note: Paragraph numbers below refer to the Annex's own numbering.

entries.t: Background as for the main Commentary. The pre-2010 Article was interpreted in light of those parts of the 2008 report that did not conflict with the earlier Commentary.
Paragraph 1 (same principles): no tax without a PE, no general force of attraction, and each source of income is tested separately. Controlled foreign company rules are not restricted.

Paragraph 2: profits are those the PE would make as a distinct and separate enterprise dealing independently. Start from the PE's trading accounts and adjust them to arm's length using a functional and factual analysis. Documented internal arrangements are a useful starting point if they reflect real functions.
Transfers of assets between a PE and other parts of the enterprise may give rise to profit. Timing issues can be resolved through the mutual agreement procedure.
Construction-site PEs: profits from goods supplied, or services performed, by other parts of the enterprise are not attributable to the site.

Dependent-agent PEs follow the same attribution principles. The agent and the enterprise are two separate potential taxpayers: the agent is taxed on its own profits, and the deemed PE is attributed profit for the functions the agent performs for the enterprise, together with the related assets and risks of the enterprise.

Paragraph 3 (deductions): expenses incurred for the PE's purposes, including executive and general administrative expenses, are deductible wherever incurred. There is no difference in principle with the arm's length approach of paragraph 2. Domestic law then decides whether the attributed expenses are deductible.

Whether a cost relates to the PE depends on the function performed. Goods supplied for resale are normally priced at arm's length. Internal royalties for intangibles should not be charged, and costs are shared instead. Services that are the PE's main activity may carry a profit mark-up, but general management services are usually charged at cost.

Whether profit should be deemed to arise from 'good management' at head office is discussed, using the extreme case of a head office that only hosts board meetings. If one State allocates such a share to head office and the other does not, the total taxed can exceed the enterprise's profits and cause double taxation.
Interest on internal 'loans' from head office is generally not deductible, except for banks.

Interest on the enterprise's real debts relating to the PE: the old direct or indirect apportionment of actual debt charges proved impractical. The guidance instead looks to a capital structure suited to the PE's functions, attributing 'free' capital. Members agreed a practical solution: for computing double tax relief, the residence State accepts the PE State's capital attribution if the difference comes from conflicting domestic methods and the PE State used an authorised approach that gives an arm's length result.
Banks may deduct internal interest on advances, since lending is their business. Insurers' investment assets follow Part IV of the report.

Paragraph 4 allowed apportionment of total profits where customary, as an exception to the separate-accounts method. It must give a result in line with paragraph 2, and the basis (turnover, expenses, capital) must suit the business.
Paragraph 5 (mere purchase): a PE that also buys goods for the enterprise is not attributed profit for that purchasing, and expenses of purchasing are not deducted.
Paragraph 6: the attribution method should not change from year to year just because another method is more favourable in a particular year.
Paragraph 7: specific Articles take priority. Equipment leasing and former Article 14 income now fall under this Article.

membersNote: Paragraphs 78 to 84 are members' observations and paragraphs 85 to 104 are their reservations on the current Article. The Annex has its own observations and reservations (Annex paragraphs 65 to 83). Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(7). Those relevant to your treaty appear in the Other countries tab.
